morning.title: Milt Windler, NASA flight director who helped save Apollo 13, dies at 94
morning.text:
Milt Windler, one of the four leaders of Mission Control who in 1970 directed the round-the-clock efforts to bring the Apollo 13 astronauts back to Earth safely, has died at the age of 94.

Windler died on Thursday, surrounded by his loving family, according to a brief notice posted online.

Named a NASA flight director in 1968 after working on recovery operations during the Mercury and Gemini programs, Windler also led a shift of flight controllers for the Apollo 8 first circumlunar flight and Apollo 10 lunar landing dress rehearsal, as well as the second, third and fourth moon landings — Apollo 12, Apollo 14 and Apollo 15. He then served as a flight director for all three crewed missions to the United States' first space station, Skylab.

morning.title: Tejas Mk2 Gains Focus as IAF Chief Flags Mk1A Delays
morning.text:
IAF Chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh on Saturday said that the delivery of the Tejas fighter jet Mk-1A version has been delayed more than expected. He also indicated that the Indian Air Force is also considering the Mk-2 version of this aircraft to address the current capability deficiencies.
On the question of imposing a penalty on Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) for the delay in the delivery of LCA Mk-1A, Singh said that delays can happen in defence programmes, but he admitted that the current delay is too much. The IAF Chief said that it happens that you plan something, but the work gets delayed. But this time the delay has been too much. We are also considering the Mark 2. It will be able to address all the current deficiencies.
In his press conference marking the 94th anniversary of the Indian Air Force, Singh stressed the importance of self-reliance in defense production and said that the country needs to reduce its dependence on foreign sources amid conflicts and disruptions to global supply chains. Singh said that self-reliance is a vital need in today’s times. And for us, it is a necessity. Self-reliance is a necessity.
He cited India’s ongoing indigenous projects as part of its efforts towards self-reliance in the defense sector, specifically citing the LCA program (which includes the Mk-1A and Mk-2 variants) and the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) program. Speaking about these indigenous programs, Singh said, “Our involvement remains consistent and we are providing full support.”

Anthropic's super bug-hunting model Mythos is hardcore good at math, as latest vuln under attack shows
morning.text: The second Anthropic-linked vulnerability known to have been exploited in the wild saw initial activity from an IP address in China targeting vulnerable hosts in the US and Japan. The vuln is a critical authentication-bypass bug in Rejetto HTTP File Server (HFS) that can lead to full admin access and remote code execution. HFS is an open source web file server that previously appeared on the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities in 2024. On Wednesday, researcher Zach Hanley at AI pen-testing company Horizon3 said he used Mythos to uncover a new flaw in the file server, now tracked as CVE-2026-61500. If you use Rejetto HFS, be sure to update to v3.2.1 or later, which fixes this and other security flaws. Hanley also published a video showing the steps to exploit HFS and remotely execute code on the server. By the next day, the CVE was under exploitation. “We started detecting exploitation of CVE-2026-61500 in Rejetto HFS this evening,” VulnCheck security researcher Patrick Garrity posted on LinkedIn on Thursday, adding that Hanley and team reported the bug to VulnCheck for CVE assignment. “Our canaries detected an actor in China targeting real vulnerable hosts in the US,” Garrity added. Garrity has been tracking CVEs attributed to Mythos and Project Glasswing, Anthropic’s initiative to give select partners access to the bug-hunting model, since shortly after the program was announced in April. Anthropic claims that Mythos is too powerful to release to the general public (insert evil laugh). As of Friday, Mythos and Project Glasswing have uncovered 286 CVEs, according to Garrity’s tracker, and up until Thursday only one of these bugs had been exploited in real-world attacks. The Thursday night activity originated from one IP address in China and targeted vulnerable servers in the US and Japan, Garrity told The Register. “Today we have seen four hits,” he told us on Friday. These originated from two different IP addresses in the US: 173.239.211[.]248 and 173.239.211[.]249. Both are in the same subnet, and “appear to be coming from a proxy,” Garrity added. China-linked digital intruders routinely use compromised devices as proxies to route malicious traffic and disguise the attackers’ true location, and in April a 10-country security advisory warned of China-nexus cyber operatives using proxy networks “strategically, and at scale.” In his write-up, Hanley said Horizon3 has used Mythos in its vulnerability research – and discovered “many critical vulnerabilities” – ever since the security company joined Project Glasswing in July. Mythos' mad math skillz CVE-2026-61500 highlights a couple of Mythos capabilities that make it really good at uncovering vulnerabilities, according to Hanley. Namely, Mythos excels at mathematical distillations and scientific tasks, especially those relating to computer science and operating systems. Finding this CVE “speaks to Mythos’s capabilities in understanding of mathematics, how it identified an exploitable set of cryptographic missteps, and approached solving the constraints to achieve remote code execution,” Hanley wrote. The security issue stems from how HFS authenticates users. It generates a random value with Math.random() and then passes this value to Koa, the Node.js web framework foundation for HFS. Koa uses keygrip to sign all session cookies with that random value. This means that if an “attacker can derive what the session signing key is, they can forge valid session cookies,” Hanley said. This should not be possible, assuming Math.random() uses a secure pseudo random number generator (PRNG). But V8’s Math.random() did not use a secure PRNG. Mythos discovered that the output of the xorshift128+ algorithm it used was fully reversible – and the application was leaking Math.random() outputs. The model’s analysis claimed that Z3, a Microsoft-developed, publicly available Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solver, could be used to recover the PRNG seed. Hanley notes that Horizon3’s researchers could not recall seeing an SMT solver used this way to attack a cryptographic flaw in a real application and bypass authentication. “What makes this impressive is that Mythos didn’t just flag the insecure PRNG in isolation – it simultaneously identified that the application leaked raw Math.random() outputs through a separate code path, recognized those two facts as a chain, and determined the leak produced exactly the observations needed to make state recovery feasible,” he wrote.®

morning.title: Pakistan's govt serves at mercy of their Army: India
What Two Pakistani Papers Reveal About India’s Strategic Gaps
morning.text:
wo recently published papers in Pakistani strategic journals explore entirely different realms of India’s national-security strategy. One assesses the art of information warfare between India and Pakistan, while the other analyses the concept of Atmanirbharta (economic and defence self-reliance).
However, upon close inspection, the papers demonstrate not only what India does wrong in the eyes of Pakistani analysts but also where India’s strategic culture allows Pakistan to interpret events and advance its security perceptions The first of the two papers, titled Weaponizing Information: A Study of Disinformation and Information Warfare between India and Pakistan , was published in Margalla Papers , a journal of Pakistan’s National Defence University. The paper, written by Gull-e-Areeba and Ahmed Waqas Waheed, employed a social constructivist methodology to analyse the information war around the 2019 Pulwama crisis and the May 2025 conflict.
The second paper, Political Construction of Atmanirbharta under Modi: Challenges and Constraints , was published in the Summer 2026 issue of Strategic Perspectives . It uses a similar social constructivist approach to analyse the narrative around India’s Atmanirbharta doctrine. The information-warfare paper assesses both sides’ perceptions of the narrative, but its emphasis is on India’s disinformation and propaganda. Likewise, the analysis of Atmanirbharta views this policy as an expression of identity politics.
- Build the Record, Not Just the Rebuttal
India’s best response to the critiques of its strategic narrative is a substantial body of research that documents similar accusations against Pakistan. For instance, the 2026 Beyond the Kinetic paper by Lt Gen D.S. Hooda and Lt Col Pavithran Rajan provides an in-depth understanding of contemporary information warfare, which is increasingly reliant on socio-technical-cognitive systems. Similarly, the Observer Research Foundation published a report in 2025 on Pakistan’s information-warfare ecosystem and its implications for India.
Thus, India should build its own research-informed strategic narratives that seek to document not only Pakistan’s accusations but also regional security dynamics at large.
- Credibility Is a Strategic Asset
While information warfare relies heavily on propaganda and perception management, counter-narratives require timely, effective, and easily verifiable dissemination. At the time of a crisis, a single misleading official statement, unsubstantiated TV commentary, or an uncorroborated tweet can fuel adversarial narratives for years. The solution is not simply increased outreach but higher credibility of one’s communication.
The more official information is distributed through channels that provide opportunities for journalists, researchers, and other governments to verify it, the more such information resists propaganda.
- Fix the Vulnerabilities Instead of Arguing About Them
Critiques of India’s defence-industrial policy may include both unsubstantiated allegations and hard facts that cannot be ignored. India’s CAG reports series contain many examples of defence procurement and R&D contracts that involved significant delays, cost overruns, and/or technology shortcomings.
For example, a 2015 CAG audit highlighted that all 14 DRDO Mission Mode Projects were delivered either delayed or exceeded their budget, and some failed to meet user requirements. Similar concerns were raised in subsequent CAG reports regarding indigenous UAV development. Thus, India must address these credibility gaps by fixing defence-industry vulnerabilities and providing verifiable examples of technological self-sufficiency.
- Explain Atmanirbharta in Strategic Terms
India’s Atmanirbharta narrative is inherently linked to Modi’s political capital, both nationally and internationally. However, Pakistan’s critiques highlight not only the domestic popularity of this campaign but also its military-industrial shortcomings. This is not surprising, given that Atmanirbharta encompasses not only military capabilities but also India’s broader economic and strategic ambitions.
Nevertheless, Pakistan’s analysts overlook India’s achievements in building strategic partnerships, promoting domestic manufacturing, and supplying critical technologies to third-party countries. The more India demonstrates its military-industrial capabilities, the less Atmanirbharta will be conflated with India’s domestic politics.
- Prepare for Information-Domain Diplomacy
The challenge of disinformation and strategic deception will increasingly shape India’s diplomacy and multilateral engagements. Therefore, India needs strategic principles that articulate its red lines on measures to build strategic trust in the information domain.
For example, future India-Pakistan CBMs negotiations may involve confidence-building measures (CBMs) in the information domain, such as joint commissions on disinformation, rapid reaction mechanisms to false information, etc. However, the experience of India-Pakistan CBMs negotiations shows that both sides must develop substantive verification measures.
The Lahore Declaration and the accompanying Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on bilateral nuclear risk reduction were adopted following intense diplomatic consultations in 1999. However, the confidence-building measures, including conventional and nuclear CBMs, were complicated by the Kargil conflict.
- Build Trusted Verification Capacity
The final lesson is related to verifiable on-the-ground evidence. Deepfakes, videos, and images of alleged events can go viral in a matter of hours and impact strategic decision-making. At the state level, such evidence requires thorough fact-checking by official resources, and foreign governments, journalists, and researchers must be able to trust this process.
Therefore, India must invest in building technical verification expertise while also engaging with academia, media, and international fact-checking organisations to ensure that its information-security practices meet global standards.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

Drones for IAF are not revolutionary but evolutionary, says IAF chief
morning.text:
New Delhi: Underlining that drones for the Indian Air Force (IAF) are not revolutionary but evolutionary since they have been in use with them for over two decades, Air Chief Marshal A P Singh said on Saturday there is no need for any separate dedicated force for unmanned systems.
He underlined that unmanned systems need to be integrated with fighters, and missiles and other weapons rather than operated as standalone capabilities.
“Drones are not revolutionary for the Indian Air Force. Yes, they are evolutionary,” Singh said in response to a question at the annual press conference ahead of Air Force Day on 8 October.
He said the IAF has had drone-related capabilities for decades and is now increasing the number and types of unmanned platforms as their role in warfare expands.
Asked whether the IAF was considering a separate drone force, Singh said, “Whether we need a separate drone force, I don’t think so.”
“They should be a part of the same setup and you have to be operating together. These have to be together along with other weapons so that they bring in that effect,” he said.
He added, “We cannot be operating one type of weapon only separately, somewhere, and one type of weapon separate. So we have not thought of having a separate force, not at all.”
He was responding to a query on whether the IAF will follow the Army’s strategy of creating exclusive drone formations.
The IAF chief gave the example of Operation Sindoor and underlined that the combined use of drones, fighters and other weapons ensured that the war ended within four days on their own terms.
He said that wars seeing only drone tactics have been going on for a long time.
India is developing a range of indigenous unmanned systems and technologies, with drones increasingly being incorporated into military operations.
This has led many to speculate that drones will lead to an era of manned fighter aircraft.
The IAF’s view is that drones cannot replace conventional combat aircraft or existing weapon systems. Instead, unmanned platforms are expected to operate alongside them as part of an integrated combat architecture.
(Edited by Ajeet Tiwari)

IAF chief says ‘delays hurt us’, calls for fewer projects, tighter delivery schedule
morning.text:
New Delhi: Indian Air Force (IAF) chief Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh has flagged the lack of concrete progress in some indigenous defence programmes, saying “delays hurt” the capabilities of the force.
Addressing the annual press conference ahead of the Air Force Day on 8 October, he said modernisation projects need to be prioritised, and wondered if the country should have another Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA), which is currently handling multiple projects at once (Tejas MK1A, Tejas Mk2, Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft, Twin Engine Deck Based Fighter, among others).
The IAF chief, who will superannuate at the end of this month, said the force supports indigenous programmes, but added that several projects are progressing at different speeds. The ecosystem, he said, could not afford to spread its limited resources too thin.
“There is a requirement to reduce the number of programmes which are going on at any time, no doubt,” Singh said, responding to a question. When one organisation handles multiple programmes, he added, it could limit the resources dedicated to each. “If the same group is involved in two programmes, obviously, there is time sharing going on,” he said.
Singh said the focus should instead be on giving clear priority to certain programmes and ensuring that tangible progress is delivered.
The comments come at a time when the IAF is pursuing several major indigenous programmes, including the Tejas Mk-1A, Tejas Mk-2, and the fifth-generation Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), while simultaneously seeking additional aircraft to arrest the decline in its fighter squadron strength.
Singh said the different programmes under development at present will eventually help address the capability gaps faced by the IAF, but acknowledged that some of these platforms will take time to become operational.
“…the MRFA (Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft), we also are looking hopefully towards Mk2. And all these will be able to fill in the gaps that exist and are likely in the near future,” he said.
He said there is some time before the AMCA reaches the sky and becomes operational. “So we’ll have to see how it progresses.”
‘We have to fill the gap’
The air chief’s comments are significant because the IAF is already dealing with a gap between its present requirements and the time required for new indigenous fighter programmes to mature.
He said that if there were delays in AMCA, the IAF will have to examine other platforms to bridge the gap. “As far as other platforms are concerned, we have to look at some platform in case there are delays in the AMCA. If we have to fill in the gap… we need to look at something,” Singh said.
However, he made it clear that no decision has been taken on any particular alternative platform.
The comments come amid Russia;s push for its Su-57 fifth-generation fighter as a possible option for India, but Singh did not commit the IAF to the Russian aircraft or any other foreign platform.
The IAF chief also stressed that India’s fighter requirement cannot be met by relying on a single aircraft type. “One aircraft cannot do all that we want,” he said, arguing that the force needs a mix of different fighter platforms.
In the near term, he said, the IAF’s fighter fleet will comprise a mix involving Tejas Mk-1A and Tejas Mk-2, the MRFA and the AMCA.
Singh also talked about the scale of aircraft production required to stop the decline in the IAF’s fighter fleet. The service, he said, requires the induction of around 36-40 fighter aircraft every year merely to prevent its squadron strength from continuing to fall.
He suggested that if production targets for Tejas (24 aircraft a year) and the MRFA (12 per year), as well as 12 additional Sukhois, move ahead, annual inductions could eventually reach the 32-40 aircraft range.
The IAF currently has several fighter programmes at different stages, with the service counting on faster deliveries of Tejas Mk-1A while simultaneously waiting for the more advanced Mk-2 and AMCA programmes to mature.
Reiterating the force’s support for indigenous programmes, he said the decisions being taken today will have consequences several years down the line. “These are the things which actually make us (capable) up near,” he said, stressing the need for decisions to be taken with a long-term view.
The Air Chief said the objective was not to abandon indigenous programmes but to prioritise them better, with organisations and teams given clearer ownership so that projects do not compete for the same resources.
The IAF has in recent years increasingly pushed for greater domestic production even as it seeks urgent solutions for its fighter shortage.

morning.title: Clever database, but can it run Doom?
morning.text: "Can it run Doom?" now applies to databases, as the author of DOOMQL has released a far more visually accurate port. There's a saying: "Be careful what you wish for." In 2025, we wrote a piece about a database boffin coming up with a version of Doom that was written in SQL. It was neat, but the visuals were nearer to 3D Monster Maze than to the 90s pixel blaster. We commented, "If persuading SQL to do the entire rendering pipeline is a 'bad idea,' we cannot wait for a terrible one." And so here we are. The author, Lukas Vogel, has been at it again and ported both Doom's game logic and renderer to SQL, running it in a database. Python handles timing, keyboard input, and bitmap display, but the rest comes from SQL queries and the CedarDB database. DOOMQL was an undeniably impressive thing. However, Vogel told The Register, "Someone on Hacker News complained last year when I did the first iteration that that one was more Wolfenstein-like because I used raycasting instead of BSP-tree traversal which was *the thing* that made Doom revolutionary. "So I obviously couldn't let that stand." Which brings us to SQLDoom. Doom, ported to SQL. In his blog, Vogel noted the ground rules for the port. Unlike DOOMQL, this had to look like real Doom. The rendering had to be purely SQL-based: "the only acceptable SQL output is a table or a bitmap encoding exact RGB values for every pixel," and the game loop also had to be purely SQL-based. Vogel told us, "I was very thrilled to find out that porting the real Doom was a) feasible and b) the performance was actually *better* than the much more barebones approach from last year! "Also, at some point I started actually playing it for fun in my free time, which is still a very strange feeling. I intended it as a tech demo, but it just feels like the real Doom, even though it doesn't share a single line of code with any existing Doom port. So I wanted to see how far I could take it. "In the end, I even got deathmatch to work." According to Vogel, the game is perfectly playable on his laptop (using a Ryzen 7 7840U), and multiplayer games can be played online using EU and US servers. We found the server performance a little sluggish – likely more due to the servers than the port – although getting SQL to jump through these hoops is something that, only a few short years ago, would be unimaginable. It's worth keeping in mind that this is a thinly veiled demonstration of the capabilities of CedarDB. It's a compiling database system where complex queries are eventually compiled to machine code. Still, it's hard not to get swept up in Vogel's enthusiasm and the fact that this is Doom… running in a database. Certainly this is a lot more fun than recreating yet another online store for yet another interminable keynote. ®

morning.title: Israel’s defence exports soar 130% despite wars, UAE biggest buyer among Abraham Accord partners—IISS
morning.text:
New Delhi: Israel’s wars across the region have far from slowed its defence exports. Instead, sales more than doubled between 2020 and 2025, with Abraham Accords partners emerging as an increasingly important market. A new report by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) shows Israeli defence exports rose 130 percent from $8.3 billion in 2020 to $19.2 billion in 2025, with the UAE, Morocco and Bahrain accounting for a growing share.
A IISS report, titled ‘Defence Dividends of the Abraham Accords’, shows that the UAE has benefited the most from the Abraham Accords. The report was released on 1 October.
The IISS report states that on a global scale, Israeli defence exports have risen even at a time Israel was busy fighting wars against Hamas, Hizbullah, Ansarullah (the Houthis), and Iran.
Abraham Accords signatories—the UAE, Bahrain and Morocco—received exports worth about $8.8 billion. While the percentage of Israeli defence exports to these three countries was nil in 2020, it rose to 7 percent in 2021 and jumped to 24 percent in 2022, before falling to 3 percent in 2023 after the Hamas 3 October attack and then rising again to 12 percent and 15 percent in 2024 and 2025, respectively, according to the IISS report.
Similarly, the value of Israeli defence exports to these countries rose to $0.79 billion in 2021 from zero in 2020, to $3.01 billion in 2022, descending to $0.33 billion in 2023 and thereafter rising again to $1.77 billion and $2.88 billion in 2024 and 2025, respectively, according to the IISS report.
Defence exports to the UAE, confirmed and alleged
The IISS report states that the UAE has been the recipient of most of Israel’s defence exports. For instance, in 2022, Israel’s Rafael Advanced Defence Systems sold medium-range SP-SAM (Spyder-MR) to the UAE. Similarly, in the same year, Elbit Systems, DSIT and Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), all Israeli defence firms, exported to the Emirates airborne defence and EW systems (DIRCM), underwater sonar and medium-range SP-SAM systems (Barak LRAD). These purchases have been confirmed.
Other reports claim Israeli firm Skylock Systems of the Avnon Group also sold the Counter-UAV system (Skylock Dome) in 2022. Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest private defence manufacturer, also reportedly sold ISR heavy UAV (Hermes 900) and a SIGINT aircraft the same year.
Reports also suggest the UAE received airborne defence and EW (DIRCM) systems from Elbit in 2025. In November 2025, Elbit signed a $2.3 billion contract with an unnamed client for the joint development of an electronic defence system to protect civil and military aircraft, with Intelligence Online reporting the country to be the UAE.
Leaked emails from Elbit sent between 2021 and early 2023 exposed the company’s efforts to sell six Hermes 900 UAVs to the UAE, with intent to expand the sale to 45 UAVs valued at around US $1.3 billion.
A document also showed the UAE requesting two crewed and two uncrewed signals intelligence aircraft, and references to SkyStriker loitering munitions, unspecified kits and Hermes 650 UAV.
Growing Israel-UAE defence-industrial cooperation
The war in Iran and Iranian attacks on the UAE have particularly helped strengthen the bond between Israelis and the Emiratis, despite unease over the Gaza conflict. Adding to that, rising tensions between the UAE and Saudi Arabia and the recently signed Mecca Pact are birthing two new defence ecosystems—Israel, the UAE, and their close ally India on one hand, and Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan on the other.
As defence ties have grown, Israeli defence manufacturers Elbit, CONTROP, Rafael, Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI)’s subsidiary Belgian Advanced Technology Systems, and Avnon Group have all established offices in the UAE.
UAE’s EDGE group and Strategic Development Fund, later incorporated into EDGE itself, have boosted cooperation with Israeli counterparts, investing in at least eight Israeli firms, such as an investment of US $10 million in 2025 to buy a 30 percent stake in ThirdEye Systems and promising to invest an additional US $12 million into a new joint venture to develop and market ThirdEye’s AI-based electro-optical recognition products.
EDGE’s Electro-Optics Centre of Excellence has partnerships with IAI and Elbit, with another EDGE subsidiary, Phantom Labs, employing the software of High Lander, an Israeli firm, while receiving a US $14 million investment from EDGE in 2023. EDGE has also signed other agreements with Israeli firms IAI and XM Cyber to develop c-UAV systems and uncrewed surface vessels and to enhance cyber capabilities, respectively.
Other Emirati companies such as G42, Spire Solutions and Resource Industries have also developed ties with Israeli firms Rafael, XM Cyber and D-Fend, respectively.
Israel and the UAE’s blossoming relationship goes beyond defence exports and imports. The two countries reportedly also founded a fund in May 2026 with an aim to jointly buy and develop new weapons systems, focusing specifically on c-UAV and other air defence systems.
Israel has also reportedly deployed to the Emirates an Iron Dome battery, a version of the Iron Beam laser air-defence system, the Spectro drone-detection surveillance system and provided intelligence on Iranian missile launches targeting the UAE, with Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu’s office revealing his visit to the Emirates, whose foreign ministry has, however, denied it.
In 2020, G42 partnered with Rafael to form Presight AI, a joint venture to commercialise AI and big-data tech. Emirati firm Spire Solutions struck up a partnership with XM Cyber in 2021 for insights into the Middle Eastern market. The Technology Innovation Institute, UAE’s premier research institution, said it would open an AI and infrared-technology research centre in Haifa.
Supporting actors—Morocco and Bahrain
Morocco and Bahrain, also part of the accords, have gained less than the UAE in their relationship with Israel. Confirmed sales to Morocco consist of Short Range SAM (Barak MX) by IAI and WanderB UAV by BlueBird Aero Systems in 2022, ISR satellite (Ofeq-13) procured from IAI in 2024 and ATMOS 2000 self-propelled artillery in 2025.
Reported but unconfirmed transfers include Hermes 900 UAVs; Harop and SpyX one-way-attack UAVs; Skylock Dome c-UAV systems; Spike self-propelled anti-tank missiles; and UT30 MK2 unmanned turrets.
Bahrain has confirmed purchases of HUD display units from Elbit in 2020 and a coastal radar from BATS (IAI) in 2021. Excluding a production facility set up by BlueBird Aero Systems in Rabat, Morocco and Bahrain are yet to cultivate defence-industrial cooperation with Israel because of funding constraints and due to the lack of a less developed defence-industrial base than their Abraham Accords partner, the Emirates.
(Edited by Viny Mishra)

morning.title: Why India may be better off without wealth tax
Palantir's fondness for French food cooked up tech's latest fad – forward-deployed engineers
morning.text: “I always laugh at the IT industry’s terms,” says Ryan Sheehan, a senior vice president at $16 billion global solutions integrator SHI. And right now the jargon that gets him giggling is “forward-deployed engineer” (FDE) because, as he told The Register at VMware's September Explore conference, “We have been doing FDE for a long time.” “Doing FDE” involves sending top consultants to a client, without tying them to a project. Instead they get a mission to build something valuable using new technology, and carte blanche to make that happen in a hurry. Sheehan has company in believing FDEs aren’t fundamentally new. Cloud monitoring vendor DoIT told The Register it has used FDEs since 2011, but only started using the term in the last quarter of 2025, when it changed the name of its “Customer Reliability Engineering” practice to FDE. That decision came as services companies adopted the term FDE to describe the work needed to build AI proofs of concept. The name has its origins at Palantir, whose chief technology officer Shyam Sankar claims he coined it in 2007 after a conversation in which his CEO Alex Karp asked him why French restaurants are so good. Karp apparently answered his own question by saying, “The wait staff is actually part of the kitchen staff. They intimately understand the food, the methodology, and the technique. They are not merely carrying the food from the kitchen to the table, but are instead part of a subtle and complex system that affects kitchen operations.” Sankar says Karp asked him “to build that, but for engineering” so he did and called it “forward deployed engineering.” “FDEs embed alongside our customers and work to ensure our software solves their problem and not some proxy for their problem,” Sankar wrote on his personal Substack. “They’re crazy enough to get on a last-minute plane to Iraq, they’re smart enough to ship quality, same-day code, and their EQ is still high enough to talk to users (and maybe even enjoy it).” Sankar says Palantir’s investors thought FDEs were a bad idea because the costs they incurred ate into margins, but says they’re worth it because they ensure customers understand the company’s products and how to get value from them. “We didn’t believe in throwing our software over the wall in the hopes the customer would divine the correct meaning from it,” Shankar wrote. “This approach built an engineering organization with unmatched creativity, responsiveness, and focus on the primacy of winning.” AWS likes winning, too, and in June announced a dedicated AWS FDE organization, and $1 billion to fund it. In July Microsoft trumped that with a $2.5 billion so-called “Frontier Company” it claims “goes beyond” FDEs. Both companies see FDEs as a way to get their consultants into customers to help them build AI apps. They argue FDEs’ time has come because, as Palantir found when users struggled to put its software to work, organizations often struggle to turn AI experiments into production applications. Stop us if you've heard this one before But vendors also admit that FDEs aren’t entirely new. Indeed, AWS told The Register it has offered customers something very similar to an FDE for years. “We started this journey all the way back in 2017 when the focus was machine learning (ML),” said Taimur Rashid, the cloud giant’s managing director for go to market, Frontier AI Engineering & Services. “We created a team called the ML Solutions Lab. The idea was that the tech is new, customers need to navigate it. So we said ‘Why don’t we loan them a data scientist?’ They can build a PoC, and the customer can build on our platform.” Rashid says AWS sometimes called this sort of arrangement a “secondment,” a “resident architect” or a “resident scientist.” Whatever you call it, Rashid said the approach worked well so AWS decided to evolve it when generative AI burst onto the scene – this time using an applied scientist and a strategist, and an evolved approach. “We forward-deploy them – they will help to identify the art of the possible and develop the solution for you or with you,” Rashid explained. “They will be part of your business and operational workflows, and effectively be yours for a defined time,” he said. That’s different to conventional services engagements, he argues, because there’s no scope of work, no hourly charge for consultants’ services. “What is different about FDE is you are saying the customer wants to build. The path is not determined.” Carlos Pereira, a Fellow and Chief Architect in Cisco’s Customer Experience team, also admited FDEs aren’t entirely new, but argued AI makes them more valuable than conventional consultants. "The idea of an expert being embedded on-site to help a customer adopt new technology and solutions isn't new,” he told The Register by email. “Our Customer Success organization has been doing this for years.” “The evolution is that AI is now a key part of that equation,” he added. “It introduces new variables like non-deterministic AI models, evaluations, faster-moving requirements, and specialized skills that not every customer team has in-house.” Analyst firms Gartner and Forrester agree that FDEs can be useful, and that this form of IT services differs due to greater intimacy between client and consultant. “They often have full-stack access to the customer’s environment and the vendor’s codebase, allowing them to build and iterate in real time,” Gartner’s Arun Chandrasekaran and Robert Thanaraj wrote in March guidance titled “An AI Leader’s Guide to Forward Deployed Engineering to Scale AI.” A June best practice report from five Forrester analysts, titled “Forward-Deployed Engineers: Use provider-embedded builders to improve outcomes,” praises the model for helping to “accelerate adoption and turn complex platforms into production-ready outcomes.” Yet both analyst firms also warn that using FDEs may see clients develop a dependency on the vendor that provides them. “The allure of delivering outcomes at speed can induce blind spots and is fraught with risks,” according to Forrester. “Without the appropriate guardrails on tech architecture and stack choices, teams can fall into a bespoke trap, where highly tailored solutions deepen vendor dependence and make future change costly.” Debt and dependency Gartner urges would-be hirers of FDEs to “beware of ill-conceived FDE engagements that can lead to a high degree of vendor dependency, security/data risk exposure, technical debt, and talent atrophy.” The latter happens when organizations hire FDEs but don’t train their own teams on new tech. “Your internal team may become operators of a black box rather than architects, making it difficult to innovate without the vendor,” Gartner warns. Gartner also worries FDEs can be a fast-track to technical debt. “A major concern with the FDE model is that it relies heavily on manually designed structures and hard-coded domain knowledge. Such human-engineered components tend to deliver short-term gains but are repeatedly superseded as more general, scalable learning systems improve.” “As large language models continue to advance, much of this manually encoded logic is likely to be rendered obsolete, requiring costly rework or full redesign, and creating a long-term technical and organizational burden.” FDEs themselves may soon be obsolete, because they’re not vendors’ only bet on improving AI consultancy skills, according to Omdia chief analyst Jay McBain. “At the same time as investing in FDEs, the big players have been investing big into partner enablement,” he told The Register. “They are playing both ends.” The tech services channel doesn’t mind that, because according to Omdia data 82 percent of partners report they “aren’t ready” to quickly grow their AI services. The vendors promoting FDEs, meanwhile, don’t want to use this form of consultancy for long. “None of these companies’ investors want to dilute a low-value services business into the overall revenue,” McBain wrote. “We are predicting all of this FDE investment will fall back into the channel by 2031 when this matures.” Which rather suggests that in a few years we’ll all be laughing at how Palantir re-heated an old form of tech services under a new name, and the rest of the industry decided to follow the same recipe. ®
